title: AI Use and Verification
text: This page is a work log, not a second report. Short bullets are welcome. It is separate from the final case study and does not count toward the 750 to 1,000 word range.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Starting point
AI system and date: Claude (Anthropic), Claude Opus 5.5 in the Claude app; November 5, 6, and 10, 2026.

Question: After controlling for genre, how strongly are a track’s audio features associated with its Spotify popularity score, and how much additional explanatory power do they provide beyond genre? (Motivation: can a hit be designed through sound?)
Course-based core model: additive multiple linear regression of track_popularity (0 to 100) on playlist genre (6 levels) plus ten audio features, fit to 28,356 unique tracks from the TidyTuesday Spotify Songs data (January 2020).
Baseline result: the audio features improve on a genre-only model (partial F = 141.9 on 10 and 28,340 df, p < 0.001), but R² rises only from 0.043 to 0.089 and the residual SD is 22.6 points. Each additional minute of track length is associated with a 2.4-point lower popularity score (95% CI: 2.1 to 2.7 points lower), holding genre and the other features fixed.
Limitation or opportunity: straight-line terms miss curved patterns (popularity rises with loudness only up to about −5 dB, and danceability matters mainly above about 0.75), and in-sample R² cannot show how much sound truly adds beyond genre. A remaining question was whether the regression models were simply too rigid to find a stronger “hit formula” in the audio features.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Substantive prompts
I’m reading the TidyTuesday Spotify Songs data (2020-01-21) in R with readr::read_csv() from the raw GitHub URL. The file has 32,833 rows, but track_id is not unique because the same track appears on several playlists. I want one row per track, so I’m using distinct(track_id, .keep_all = TRUE). Is this a reasonable approach when the observational unit is a track? What are the risks of keeping only the first playlist row (for example, tracks listed under more than one genre), and how can I check how many tracks are affected?
I’m making an exploratory figure in ggplot2. For each of four audio features (duration_min, energy, loudness, danceability), I split tracks into deciles with ntile(), then compute the mean of (popularity minus the track’s genre average) in each decile with a 95% CI. I also want a shaded band showing the middle 50% of tracks in each decile. I want facets with free x-axes and a short direct label for the band and the line in the first panel only. Here is my code: [paste code]. Here is the problem I’m getting: [describe problem or paste error]. How can I fix it?
I am creating a regression case study in R and Quarto. My question is: after controlling for genre, how strongly are a track’s audio features associated with its Spotify popularity score, and how much additional explanatory power do they provide beyond genre? The broader motivation is whether a hit song can be designed through its sound. The response is track_popularity, Spotify’s 0 to 100 popularity score, treated as continuous. The main predictors are playlist genre (EDM, Latin, pop, R&B, rap, rock) and ten Spotify audio features: danceability, energy, loudness (dB), speechiness, acousticness, instrumentalness, liveness, valence, tempo (BPM), and track length (minutes). The data are 28,356 unique tracks from the TidyTuesday Spotify Songs dataset (January 2020). My course-based core model is an additive multiple linear regression of popularity on genre plus the ten audio features. For my two required course elements, I plan to use (1) natural splines and genre-by-feature interactions and (2) repeated 10-fold cross-validation comparing genre-only, linear, and spline/interaction models by RMSE. My main result so far is that the audio features improve on genre alone (partial F = 141.9 on 10 and 28,340 df, p < 0.001), but R-squared rises only from 0.043 to 0.089 and the residual SD is 22.6 points; for example, each additional minute of track length is associated with a 2.4-point lower popularity score (95% CI: 2.1 to 2.7). I found this limitation or opportunity: the linear terms miss curved patterns (loudness levels off above about -5 dB; danceability matters mainly above about 0.75), in-sample R-squared cannot show how much sound truly adds beyond genre, and 9.2% of tracks have a popularity score of exactly 0, which may reflect duplicate releases rather than true unpopularity. Suggest three feasible extensions that keep the core analysis connected to regression methods taught in my class. One option may be a model not taught in class used as a comparator. For each, explain how it strengthens the same research question, how its result would enter the final case study, the implementation steps, and two ways I could verify it. Do not choose for me.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
My decisions

Selected extension: a random forest (ranger), a tree-based model not covered in STAT 330, used as a comparator to my course-based regression models. It uses the same genre and ten audio features, and every model is compared with the same artist-grouped 10-fold cross-validation and RMSE. I chose it because it directly tests whether a more flexible model can find a “hit formula” in sound that my regression missed.
Accepted: using the same predictors, folds, and metric for every model; grouping the folds by artist (the grouped cross-validation idea from Unit 5), so the forest cannot learn an artist’s sound in training and reuse it in testing; and adding permutation importance to see which features the forest relies on.
Changed: the forest’s default settings overfit (out-of-bag RMSE 22.8), so I tuned two settings with the out-of-bag error (mtry = 3, minimum node size = 200; out-of-bag RMSE 22.3). I used one round of 10-fold cross-validation for this comparison instead of five repeats to keep rendering time reasonable.
Rejected or corrected: I did not choose the other two suggested options, a mixed-effects model with artist random intercepts and quantile regression for the top 10% of songs, because they would shift the focus away from comparing prediction with and without sound. I also kept the tracks with popularity 0, because dropping them changed the track-length coefficient by about a third without a clear reason to treat them all as errors.

Connection to the final case study: the method and result appear in the “A new direction with AI” section: a cross-validation comparison of the random forest with the regression models and a permutation-importance figure. The result supports the main answer in “What this means”: even a flexible model explains only about 11% of the variation in new songs, so the small R² of my regression is not just because the model is too simple.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Independent verification

Out-of-bag error vs. cross-validation (official documentation): the ranger documentation states that prediction.error is the out-of-bag mean squared error for regression (ranger on CRAN; Wright & Ziegler, 2017). The forest’s out-of-bag RMSE (22.31) matched my artist-grouped cross-validation RMSE (22.34) and a random-fold cross-validation RMSE (22.30). This shows that my cross-validation loop computes the error correctly and that songs by the same artist do not inflate the forest’s performance much.
Negative control (shuffled features): I shuffled the ten audio features within each genre, which breaks any real link between sound and popularity. The forest’s out-of-bag RMSE rose to 23.26, about the same as the genre-only regression (23.18). This shows that the forest’s small gain comes from real information in the audio features, not from a coding error or data leakage.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Remaining limitation
Spotify’s ten audio features are only a rough summary of sound. They do not capture lyrics, melody, hooks, or production quality, and the data are playlist songs from early 2020. So the forest’s ceiling of about 11% only shows how much these particular features can predict, not that sound in general cannot matter. Also, the forest’s settings were chosen with out-of-bag error on all songs, which may make its cross-validation error slightly optimistic.

title: Can a Hit Be Designed? Audio Features and Spotify Popularity Beyond Genre

title: Can a Hit Be Designed? Audio Features and Spotify Popularity Beyond Genre
text:
The question
These days, many songs seem to be made to go viral on TikTok and other short-video apps. Some people even say you can design a hit by choosing the right length, energy, or beat. I wanted to test this idea with data. My question is: after accounting for genre, how much are a song’s audio features related to its Spotify popularity, and how much do they add beyond genre? This matters for independent artists and small labels, who have limited time and money and must decide whether to focus on the sound or on promotion.
I used the Spotify Songs dataset from TidyTuesday (January 2020). Some songs appeared in more than one playlist, so I kept one row per song, which left 28,356 songs. The response is Spotify’s popularity score (0 to 100). The predictors are playlist genre (six genres) and ten audio features, such as track length, energy, loudness, and danceability. One limitation is that popularity is Spotify’s own score, and about 9% of songs score exactly 0. Some of these may be duplicate versions, not songs that nobody listens to.

title: Can a Hit Be Designed? Audio Features and Spotify Popularity Beyond Genre
text:
What the baseline shows


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(splines)   # for natural splines, ns()


spotify_raw <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-01-21/spotify_songs.csv")

# Some tracks appear on several playlists, so keep one row per track
songs <- spotify_raw |>
  distinct(track_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(duration_min = duration_ms / 60000)   # milliseconds -> minutes

genre_only <- lm(track_popularity ~ playlist_genre, data = songs)

baseline <- lm(track_popularity ~ playlist_genre + danceability + energy +
                 loudness + speechiness + acousticness + instrumentalness +
                 liveness + valence + tempo + duration_min,
               data = songs)

# R-squared: genre only vs. genre + audio features
summary(genre_only)$r.squared


[1] 0.04341299


Show code
summary(baseline)$r.squared


[1] 0.08903564


Show code
anova(genre_only, baseline)                 # partial F-test


Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: track_popularity ~ playlist_genre
Model 2: track_popularity ~ playlist_genre + danceability + energy + loudness + 
    speechiness + acousticness + instrumentalness + liveness + 
    valence + tempo + duration_min
  Res.Df      RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1  28350 15238348                                  
2  28340 14511583 10    726765 141.93 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Show code
coef(baseline)["duration_min"]              # change per extra minute


duration_min

Show code

    2.5 %    97.5 % 
-2.680054 -2.141792 


Show code

[1] 22.62859




Show code
songs |>
  # Drop about 1% of tracks with extreme values so the plot is readable
  filter(loudness > -20, duration_min > 1.5, duration_min < 7.5) |>
  select(track_popularity,
         "Track length (minutes)" = duration_min,
         "Energy (0 to 1)"        = energy,
         "Loudness (dB)"          = loudness,
         "Danceability (0 to 1)"  = danceability) |>
  pivot_longer(-track_popularity, names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = track_popularity)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.03, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Popularity changes only a little with each audio feature",
       x = "Audio feature value",
       y = "Spotify popularity (0 to 100)") +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 1: Each gray dot is one track; the blue line is the average trend (with a 95% band). About 1% of tracks with extreme loudness or length are left out of the plot only.





As a starting point, I fit a multiple linear regression with genre and all ten audio features. It is simple and matches my question: because genre is in the model, each feature is compared among songs in the same genre.
The audio features help, but only a little. R-squared rose from 0.043 (genre only) to 0.089, and the partial F-test was significant (F = 141.9, p < 0.001). Track length had the clearest result. Holding genre and the other features constant, each extra minute was linked to a popularity score 2.4 points lower (95% CI: 2.1 to 2.7 points lower). So a 5-minute song is expected to score about 5 points lower than a similar 3-minute song, which is small next to the typical prediction error of about 23 points.
The baseline has two limits. It uses straight lines, but Figure 1 shows curves; for example, popularity rises with loudness only until about −5 dB. It also assumes that the length pattern is the same in every genre.

title: Can a Hit Be Designed? Audio Features and Spotify Popularity Beyond Genre
text:
Going beyond the baseline
Use two STAT 330 method families. Give each part a descriptive heading that states the question or finding, not an assignment label. Explain why you chose each method, how you checked it, and what it adds to the answer.

Shorter songs score higher in most genres, but not in rock


Show code
spline_model <- lm(track_popularity ~ playlist_genre + ns(danceability, 3) +
                     ns(energy, 3) + ns(loudness, 3) + speechiness + acousticness +
                     instrumentalness + liveness + valence + tempo + ns(duration_min, 3),
                   data = songs)

# Let the track-length curve be different in each genre
interaction_model <- lm(track_popularity ~ playlist_genre * ns(duration_min, 3) +
                          ns(danceability, 3) + ns(energy, 3) + ns(loudness, 3) +
                          speechiness + acousticness + instrumentalness + liveness +
                          valence + tempo,
                        data = songs)

anova(baseline, spline_model)            # do curves help?


Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: track_popularity ~ playlist_genre + danceability + energy + loudness + 
    speechiness + acousticness + instrumentalness + liveness + 
    valence + tempo + duration_min
Model 2: track_popularity ~ playlist_genre + ns(danceability, 3) + ns(energy, 
    3) + ns(loudness, 3) + speechiness + acousticness + instrumentalness + 
    liveness + valence + tempo + ns(duration_min, 3)

Show code
# A "typical" song: every other audio feature at its median
typical <- songs |>
  summarise(across(c(danceability, energy, loudness, speechiness, acousticness,
                     instrumentalness, liveness, valence, tempo), median))

new_songs <- expand_grid(playlist_genre = sort(unique(songs$playlist_genre)),
                         duration_min = seq(2, 6, by = 0.1),
                         typical)

pred <- predict(interaction_model, newdata = new_songs, interval = "confidence")
new_songs <- bind_cols(new_songs, as_tibble(pred))

ggplot(new_songs, aes(x = duration_min, y = fit)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ playlist_genre) +
  labs(title = "Longer songs score lower in most genres, but not in rock",
       x = "Track length (minutes)",
       y = "Predicted popularity (0 to 100)") +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 2: Predicted popularity by track length in each genre, for a song with all other features at their median. Bands are 95% confidence intervals.







Show code
# Expected change from a 3-minute to a 5-minute song in each genre, with a 95% CI
change_3_to_5 <- function(genre) {
  two_songs <- expand_grid(playlist_genre = genre, duration_min = c(3, 5), typical)
  X <- model.matrix(delete.response(terms(interaction_model)), two_songs,
                    xlev = interaction_model$xlevels)
  d <- X[2, ] - X[1, ]                                   # 5 minutes minus 3 minutes
  est <- sum(d * coef(interaction_model))
  se  <- sqrt(drop(t(d) %*% vcov(interaction_model) %*% d))
  tibble(genre, change = est, lower = est - 1.96 * se, upper = est + 1.96 * se)
}

map(sort(unique(songs$playlist_genre)), change_3_to_5) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1)))


# A tibble: 6 × 4
  genre change lower upper
  <chr>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 edm    -11.2 -13    -9.4
2 latin   -4.6  -6.7  -2.5
3 pop     -8.9 -10.9  -7  
4 r&b     -7.6  -9.5  -5.8
5 rap     -8.1  -9.8  -6.4
6 rock     0.3  -1.6   2.1


To fix the straight-line problem, I replaced the lines for length, energy, loudness, and danceability with natural splines (3 degrees of freedom each). I also let the length curve change by genre with an interaction. Both steps improved the fit (partial F = 20.8 for the splines and 8.8 for the interaction, both p < 0.001).
Figure 2 shows that the length pattern depends on genre. In EDM, a 5-minute song is expected to score about 11 points lower than a 3-minute song (95% CI: 9.4 to 13.0). Pop, rap, and R&B drop about 8 points (7.6 to 8.9), and Latin about 5. In rock, there is almost no difference (+0.3 points; 95% CI: −1.6 to 2.1). So “shorter is better” is not a general rule.


Sound adds only a little when predicting new songs


Show code
models <- list(
  "Genre only"               = track_popularity ~ playlist_genre,
  "Baseline"                 = formula(baseline),
  "Splines"                  = formula(spline_model),
  "Splines + genre x length" = formula(interaction_model)
)

set.seed(330)
cv_results <- tibble()
for (r in 1:5) {                                          # repeat 5 times
  fold <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(songs)))     # random 10 folds
  for (k in 1:10) {
    train <- songs[fold != k, ]
    test  <- songs[fold == k, ]
    for (name in names(models)) {
      fit  <- lm(models[[name]], data = train)
      pred <- predict(fit, newdata = test)
      rmse <- sqrt(mean((test$track_popularity - pred)^2))
      cv_results <- bind_rows(cv_results,
                              tibble(model = name, repeat_id = r, fold = k, rmse = rmse))
    }
  }
}

# Average prediction error for each model
cv_results |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(mean_rmse = mean(rmse),
            sd_rmse   = sd(rmse),
            cv_r2     = 1 - mean(rmse^2) / var(songs$track_popularity)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_rmse))


# A tibble: 4 × 4
  model                    mean_rmse sd_rmse  cv_r2
  <chr>                        <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Genre only                    23.2   0.183 0.0430
2 Baseline                      22.6   0.162 0.0881
3 Splines                       22.6   0.173 0.0929
4 Splines + genre x length      22.5   0.171 0.0962


Show code
# In how many of the 50 folds did the baseline beat genre only?
cv_results |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = rmse) |>
  summarise(baseline_better = sum(Baseline < `Genre only`))


# A tibble: 1 × 1
  baseline_better
            <int>
1              50


A better fit on the same data does not always mean better prediction, so I used 10-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times. Each model was fit on 90% of the songs and tested on the other 10%.
Adding the audio features lowered the prediction error (RMSE) from 23.2 to 22.6 points, and this happened in all 50 folds. The splines and the genre interaction lowered it only a little more, to 22.5. The best model explains about 10% of the variation in new songs (cross-validated R-squared = 0.096), while genre alone explains about 4%. The flexible model did not overfit, but the gain was small.

title: Can a Hit Be Designed? Audio Features and Spotify Popularity Beyond Genre
text:
A new direction with AI


Show code
library(ranger)   # random forest (not covered in STAT 330)

# 4 songs have no artist name, so use the track id for them
songs <- songs |> mutate(artist = coalesce(track_artist, track_id))

# Artist-grouped folds: all songs by one artist stay in the same fold
set.seed(330)
artists <- unique(songs$artist)
artist_folds <- tibble(artist = artists,
                       fold = sample(rep(1:10, length.out = length(artists))))
fold <- left_join(songs, artist_folds, by = "artist")$fold

rf_formula <- formula(baseline)   # same genre + 10 audio features as the baseline
rmse <- function(actual, predicted) sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))

ext_results <- tibble()
for (k in 1:10) {
  train <- songs[fold != k, ]
  test  <- songs[fold == k, ]
  # Regression models from the previous section
  for (name in names(models)) {
    fit <- lm(models[[name]], data = train)
    ext_results <- bind_rows(ext_results,
      tibble(model = name, fold = k, rmse = rmse(test$track_popularity, predict(fit, test))))
  }
  # Random forest
  forest <- ranger(rf_formula, data = train, num.trees = 300,
                   mtry = 3, min.node.size = 200, seed = 330)
  ext_results <- bind_rows(ext_results,
    tibble(model = "Random forest", fold = k,
           rmse = rmse(test$track_popularity, predict(forest, test)$predictions)))
}

ext_results |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(mean_rmse = mean(rmse),
            cv_r2     = 1 - mean(rmse^2) / var(songs$track_popularity)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_rmse))


# A tibble: 5 × 3
  model                    mean_rmse  cv_r2
  <chr>                        <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Genre only                    23.2 0.0422
2 Baseline                      22.6 0.0869
3 Splines                       22.6 0.0915
4 Splines + genre x length      22.6 0.0944
5 Random forest                 22.3 0.111 




Show code
forest_all <- ranger(rf_formula, data = songs, num.trees = 300, mtry = 3,
                     min.node.size = 200, importance = "permutation", seed = 330)

tibble(feature = names(forest_all$variable.importance),
       importance = forest_all$variable.importance) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = importance, y = reorder(feature, importance))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "The forest relies most on genre, then loudness, energy, and length",
       x = "Increase in prediction error (MSE) when the feature is shuffled",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 3: Permutation importance from a random forest fit to all songs: how much the prediction error (MSE) grows when one feature is randomly shuffled.







Show code
# Check 1: the forest's built-in out-of-bag error should match the CV error
sqrt(forest_all$prediction.error)


[1] 22.30493


Show code
# Check 2: shuffle the audio features within each genre;
# the forest should then do no better than genre alone
set.seed(331)
shuffled <- songs |>
  group_by(playlist_genre) |>
  mutate(across(c(danceability, energy, loudness, speechiness, acousticness,
                  instrumentalness, liveness, valence, tempo, duration_min), sample)) |>
  ungroup()

forest_null <- ranger(rf_formula, data = shuffled, num.trees = 300, mtry = 3,
                      min.node.size = 200, seed = 330)
sqrt(forest_null$prediction.error)   # forest with shuffled sound


[1] 23.26687


Show code
sigma(genre_only)                    # genre-only regression, for comparison


[1] 23.18422


My regression models showed that sound adds only a little. But maybe they were just too simple to find the real pattern. To test this, I used AI help to fit a random forest, a tree-based model not covered in STAT 330 that can find complex curves and interactions on its own. I gave it the same genre and ten audio features and compared it with my regression models using 10-fold cross-validation. This time I grouped the folds by artist, so songs by the same artist were never in both the training and test sets.
The random forest predicted best, but only slightly. Its RMSE was 22.3 points, compared with 22.6 for my spline and interaction model and 23.2 for genre alone, and it explained only about 11% of the variation in new songs. Figure 3 shows that it relied most on genre, then loudness, energy, and track length. I checked the result in two ways. The forest’s built-in out-of-bag error (22.3) matched my cross-validation, and when I shuffled the audio features within each genre, the forest did no better than genre alone (23.3 vs. 23.2). So even a flexible model finds little “hit formula” in these features.
Details are in the AI-use record.

title: Can a Hit Be Designed? Audio Features and Spotify Popularity Beyond Genre
text:
What this means
My answer is that sound is related to Spotify popularity, but it explains only a small part of it. The statistical evidence is strong: the audio features improved prediction in every fold, and even a flexible random forest explained only about 11% of the variation. In practice, however, they lowered the prediction error by less than one point on a 100-point scale. Track length was the most useful feature, and its pattern depended on genre: shorter songs scored higher in EDM and pop, but not in rock.
So a hit probably cannot be designed through sound alone. These results are associations, not causes, and Spotify popularity is not the same as going viral on TikTok. The data also come from playlists in early 2020. A useful next step would be to add information about promotion or the artist’s existing fan base, which may explain much more of the variation.
